The East-West Pipeline outage adds another layer to that dislocation by reducing Saudi Arabia’s ability to shift export flows between the Gulf and the Red Sea.
First, reduced westbound flexibility could force Saudi Arabia to route more crude back through Gulf export terminals and the Hormuz-linked shipping system. Reuters reported that Ras Tanura and Juaymah loaded around 22m barrels on 12 vessels during the week of September 7–13, compared with six or seven vessels in each of the previous three weeks.

Second, European refiners seeking US, Guyanese, Algerian, North Sea and other alternative grades are competing in some of the same non-Gulf supply pools that Asian refiners can use to diversify away from Middle Eastern risk.
The result is a potential increase in both crude differentials and tonne-mile demand.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues to reshape vessel deployment and cargo flows across the Middle East and South Asia.
Carriers are diverting Gulf-bound vessels to alternative hubs including Khor Fakkan, Fujairah, Sohar, and Salalah, along with ports across India and Southeast Asia.
This shift is creating localized congestion at diversion ports and increasing reliance on feeder networks and inland transport to move cargo to its final destination.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced carriers to reroute vessels away from Gulf ports and into alternative hubs across Oman, the UAE, India, and Southeast Asia.
This shift has removed capacity from the system while increasing pressure on ports that were not designed to absorb sudden volume spikes.
At Sohar, congestion formed almost immediately
At Sohar, the impact of rerouted cargo was immediate.
Vessel wait times increased, but cargo dwell increased at a much faster rate, indicating the primary constraint is no longer berth capacity but the ability to move containers out of the port.
Cargo dwell increased more than fourfold, while total port time tripled within weeks.
Salalah represents a third pattern.
Dwell times more than tripled over a two-month period, reflecting sustained accumulation rather than a single disruption event.
Rather than an immediate spike, cargo dwell times increased steadily from January through March.
They are forming at secondary ports where rerouted cargo is creating uneven pressure.

Since the outbreak of the conflict, vessel congestion around the Strait of Hormuz, the rerouting of trade flows and growing use of ship-to-ship transfers have lengthened cargo delivery times and reduced fleet efficiency, driving freight rates higher.
But rerouting cargoes or transferring them between ships ties up vessels for longer and reduces the number available for hire, causing freight rates to rise sharply.
Shipping costs had already risen following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which triggered a reshuffling of global crude and oil product trade.
By mid-October, shipping crude from West Africa to Europe on a Suezmax vessel cost over $22 per barrel, more than four times pre-conflict levels. North Sea Aframax rates also tripled, reaching over $6 per barrel.
The impact has extended into the product tanker market.
As a result, oil product cargoes have been redistributed across the fleet of smaller vessels, tightening shipping capacity throughout the product tanker market. The two types of DOD bases face the same challenge, but for different reasons. In Afghanistan, the diesel generators that provide electricity at bases are the top consumer of fuel on the battlefield.
One way to reduce that fuel use is to generate more power on site, through distributed generation technologies like solar or waste-to-power plants. Another is to use that power more efficiently. Oilfield Services Earnings Kickoff
Halliburton, SLB, Weatherford, Liberty and Oceaneering reported this week. What they said about U.S. completions pricing, the Gulf, Venezuela, deepwater and 2027, with Friday's rig count.
Oct 23, 2026
∙ Paid
4

Frac crews got price increases in the third quarter even though none of the four service companies with U.S. land businesses expects much more U.S. drilling and completion work next year. Weatherford expects North American activity to rise by low single digits in 2027.
Halliburton built its 2027 plan on a flat North America and called any frac recovery “purely upside.” Liberty CEO Ron Gusek said a return to mid-cycle economics next year “would be a step too far.” SLB called North America a low-growth market, though it expects its own business there to grow.

China Oilfield Services expanding fleet with 59 offshore vessels
China Oilfield Services Limited (COSL) has issued a procurement notice to build 59 offshore work vessels across six designs, kicking off one of China’s most substantial offshore support fleet renewal programmes in recent years.
The newbuild portfolio covers Anchor Handling Tug Supply (AHTS) vessels, Platform Supply Vessels (PSVs), and oilfield standby‑and‑supply units for diverse offshore operational scenarios.
The breakdown includes four 15,000‑hp AHTS, six 12,000‑hp AHTS, three 8,000‑hp AHTS, fourteen 2,000‑dwt PSVs, twenty‑three 3,000‑dwt PSVs, seven 4,000‑dwt PSVs, one 6,500‑hp LNG‑fuelled standby‑and‑supply vessel (3,000 dwt with oil transfer capacity), and one 10,000‑hp LNG‑fuelled standby‑and‑supply vessel (4,000 dwt with oil transfer capacity).
Delivery will be phased from 2028 through to 2030.
Upon completion, the new fleet will strengthen comprehensive logistical support for China’s offshore oil‑and‑gas operations and accelerate green, intelligent upgrading of the country’s offshore work‑vessel fleet.
Related: Seadrill loses $55m appeal over Hercules rig redelivery
In parallel to the 59‑vessel initiative, the board has also cleared feasibility work for four high‑performance jack‑up drilling platforms. These new rigs will feature upgraded well‑control systems, automated drilling modules and specialised hardware optimised for long‑horizontal‑section shale‑oil development.
